what_it_does: Large language models (LLMs) normally store their weights as 16- or 32-bit numbers, which is expensive in memory and compute. Binarization is the most extreme form of compression: each weight is rounded to either +1 or −1, so multiplications become simple logic operations. The problem is that binarizing activations (the intermediate values flowing through the network) causes severe accuracy loss, and the self-attention mechanism (the part of the model that relates every word to every other word) still requires full multiplications even after weights are binarized. XShift attacks both problems: it replaces multiplications with XNOR (a one-bit comparison) and cheap bit-shift operations, and it designs a matching hardware dataflow on programmable chips (FPGAs) — grids of reconfigurable logic — that can exploit the resulting sparsity (many zero values that can be skipped) and handle the two distinct phases of LLM operation (filling a prompt versus generating one token at a time) differently.
